questions.enonce_markdown:
Find the values of $R$ and $\alpha$, $R > 0$ and $0^\circ < \alpha < 90^\circ$, for which $4\cos\theta + 3\sin\theta \equiv R\cos(\theta - \alpha)$.

Hence, obtain the greatest value of the expression $\dfrac{1}{4\cos\theta + 3\sin\theta + 6}$, and give the corresponding value of $\theta$ between $0^\circ$ and $360^\circ$. (6 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Harmonic form.** Expand: $R\cos(\theta - \alpha) = R\cos\alpha\cos\theta + R\sin\alpha\sin\theta$. Comparing with $4\cos\theta + 3\sin\theta$:
$$R\cos\alpha = 4, \qquad R\sin\alpha = 3.$$
Squaring and adding: $R^2 = 16 + 9 = 25$, so $R = 5$ (since $R > 0$). Dividing: $\tan\alpha = \tfrac34$, so $\alpha = \tan^{-1}\tfrac34 = 36.87^\circ$ (this lies in $0^\circ < \alpha < 90^\circ$, as $\cos\alpha = \tfrac45$ and $\sin\alpha = \tfrac35$ are both positive).
$$\boxed{R = 5, \qquad \alpha = 36.87^\circ\ (36.9^\circ \text{ to 1 d.p.}),\ \text{so } 4\cos\theta + 3\sin\theta \equiv 5\cos(\theta - 36.87^\circ)}$$

**Greatest value of the fraction.** The denominator is
$$4\cos\theta + 3\sin\theta + 6 = 5\cos(\theta - \alpha) + 6.$$
Since $-1 \le \cos(\theta - \alpha) \le 1$, the denominator lies between $6 - 5 = 1$ and $6 + 5 = 11$; it is always positive, so the fraction is always defined. The fraction is greatest when the (positive) denominator is least, that is when $\cos(\theta - \alpha) = -1$:
$$\text{greatest value} = \frac{1}{6 - 5} = 1.$$
This occurs when $\theta - 36.87^\circ = 180^\circ$ (taking the value in the range $0^\circ$ to $360^\circ$): $\theta = 216.87^\circ$.

$$\boxed{\text{Greatest value} = 1, \quad\text{at } \theta = 216.9^\circ\ (216.87^\circ)}$$

**Check:** $4\cos 216.87^\circ + 3\sin 216.87^\circ = 4(-0.8) + 3(-0.6) = -5$, so the denominator is $-5 + 6 = 1$.

questions.enonce_markdown: Using De Moivre's theorem, write down the equivalent form of $\cos 3\theta + i\sin 3\theta$. Hence show that $\sin 3\theta \equiv 3\sin\theta - 4\sin^3\theta$. (6 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**De Moivre's theorem:** $(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)^n = \cos n\theta + i\sin n\theta$ for any integer $n$. With $n = 3$:
$$\boxed{\cos 3\theta + i\sin 3\theta \equiv (\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)^3}$$

**Expand** the right-hand side with the binomial theorem, using $i^2 = -1$ and $i^3 = -i$:
$$(\cos\theta + i\sin\theta)^3 = \cos^3\theta + 3\cos^2\theta\,(i\sin\theta) + 3\cos\theta\,(i\sin\theta)^2 + (i\sin\theta)^3$$
$$= \big(\cos^3\theta - 3\cos\theta\sin^2\theta\big) + i\big(3\cos^2\theta\sin\theta - \sin^3\theta\big).$$

**Equate imaginary parts** (two complex numbers are equal when their real and imaginary parts are equal):
$$\sin 3\theta \equiv 3\cos^2\theta\sin\theta - \sin^3\theta.$$
Replace $\cos^2\theta$ by $1 - \sin^2\theta$:
$$\sin 3\theta \equiv 3\sin\theta\,(1 - \sin^2\theta) - \sin^3\theta = 3\sin\theta - 3\sin^3\theta - \sin^3\theta = 3\sin\theta - 4\sin^3\theta. \qquad \blacksquare$$

(Equating real parts in the same way gives $\cos 3\theta \equiv 4\cos^3\theta - 3\cos\theta$. Check at $\theta = 30^\circ$: $\sin 90^\circ = 1$ and $3\left(\tfrac12\right) - 4\left(\tfrac18\right) = 1$.)
